en.title: Mechanical Engineering: the whole course
en.short: What mechanical engineering covers, how degrees are organised, and how to study the subject well.

sections.heading: What mechanical engineering is
sections.text: Mechanical engineering is the analysis, design, manufacture, operation and maintenance of machines and energy systems. It covers engines, turbines, pumps, vehicles, robots, heating and cooling plant, and production equipment. It matters because almost every industry depends on safe, efficient machines and on people who can choose materials, shape parts, manage heat and motion, and keep equipment running. The subject combines mathematics and science with practical judgement about cost, safety, reliability and the environment. These summaries teach principles. They do not replace design codes, standards, laboratory rules or a qualified engineer. Design codes and standards differ by country and change over time, so always use the current edition required by your institution and the law where the work is done. Numerical examples are for learning only.

sections.heading: How a degree is organised
sections.text: Length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. In Nigeria, a BEng in mechanical engineering usually takes five years and includes industrial training under SIWES, the Students Industrial Work Experience Scheme. Polytechnic students commonly take an ND, then supervised industrial work, then an HND. In most of the UK, a BEng usually takes three years and an MEng four; in Scotland each usually takes a year longer. Professional registration also differs. In Nigeria, COREN registers engineering practitioners, and registration requirements should be checked with COREN. Early years are shared with other engineers: mathematics, mechanics, drawing, materials and basic science. Later years add design, laboratories, workshops and a final-year project. A master’s degree adds advanced analysis and a dissertation.

sections.heading: The main areas, in teaching order
sections.text:
Teaching usually begins with engineering mathematics, engineering drawing and CAD, statics, dynamics, materials science, mechanics of materials under axial loading, thermodynamics, fluid mechanics, electrical and electronic principles, and engineering computing and numerical methods. These give the language and tools for later work.

Core subjects then deepen the same ideas: beams, torsion and deflection; machine elements and mechanisms; manufacturing processes; metrology and measurement; mechanical vibrations; heat transfer; applied thermodynamics and power cycles; fluid machinery and pipe systems; control systems; machine design and CAD; tribology, lubrication and wear; refrigeration and air conditioning; industrial engineering and maintenance; professional practice, ethics and registration; and an engineering project with technical communication. In Nigeria, professional practice includes awareness of COREN and the responsibilities of registered engineers. Other countries have their own regulators and codes.

At master’s level, common subjects are advanced solid mechanics and the finite element method, computational fluid dynamics, advanced thermodynamics and heat transfer, and research methods. A dissertation usually follows.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Study by solving problems, not by reading solutions. Draw a free-body diagram for forces, a control volume for fluids and thermodynamics, and a clear sketch for every machine part. Write units on every line and convert before calculating. Ask whether the answer is reasonable: a shaft should not twist by 30 degrees under normal load, and a pump should not need more power than its motor can supply. Learn typical properties and efficiencies so that errors stand out.

Use software after you can do a simple hand check. Keep a formula sheet in your own words and state assumptions. Treat laboratories, workshops and industrial training as part of the course, because they show how drawings, tolerances and standards become real parts. Read a standard only with guidance, and note its edition and country.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Common mistakes include mixing units such as N, kN, mm and m; using gauge pressure where absolute pressure is needed; confusing stress with strain; and ignoring sign conventions in forces, moments and deflections. In thermodynamics, students forget to define the system or use the wrong property table. In fluids, they forget losses or use the wrong diameter. In design, they copy a formula or standard clause without checking its conditions, units and edition. They also trust software output because it looks precise. State your assumptions and show the method, because an examiner and a senior engineer both need to see how you reached the answer.

keyPoints: Mechanical engineering covers machines, energy systems, manufacturing, controls and maintenance.
Degree length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your handbook.
Design codes, standards and registration differ by country; in Nigeria, COREN registers engineering practitioners.
Learn the hand method and draw a diagram before trusting software.
Write units on every line and check that every answer is reasonable.
Professional practice includes ethics, safety and responsibility for your designs.

en.title: Engineering mathematics for mechanical engineers
en.short: Calculus, vectors, linear algebra, ODEs and Laplace transforms applied to mechanics, thermodynamics and control.

sections.heading: Calculus and rates
sections.text:
Calculus studies change. In mechanics, velocity is v = ds/dt and acceleration is a = dv/dt; displacement is the integral of velocity. In thermodynamics, work is an integral: W = ∫F dx. A derivative gives a local rate, an integral adds small contributions.

Example: s = 3t² + 2t metres. Then v = 6t + 2 m/s and a = 6 m/s². At t = 2 s, v = 14 m/s. Displacement from t = 0 to 2 s is ∫(6t + 2)dt = [3t² + 2t] from 0 to 2 = 16 m.

sections.heading: Vectors and matrices
sections.text:
Vectors carry magnitude and direction. A force F = 3i + 4j N has magnitude √(3² + 4²) = 5 N. The dot product F·d gives work; with d = 2i + 1j m, W = 3×2 + 4×1 = 10 J.

Linear algebra solves several equations at once. A matrix stores coefficients, and Ax = b represents a system. Eigenvalues give natural frequencies and modes in vibration and stability in control.

sections.heading: Differential equations
sections.text: An ordinary differential equation (ODE) relates a function to its derivatives. Newton’s cooling law dT/dt = −k(T − T∞) is first order; its solution is T = T∞ + (T0 − T∞)e^(−kt). A mass-spring-damper follows m x″ + c x′ + kx = F(t), a second-order ODE. Solve by finding a complementary solution and a particular solution.

sections.heading: Laplace transforms
sections.text: The Laplace transform changes a function of time into a function of s. It turns derivatives into algebra: x′ becomes sX(s) − x(0). For m x″ + kx = F with zero initial conditions, (ms² + k)X = F, so the transfer function is G(s) = X(s)/F(s) = 1/(ms² + k). Control engineers use G(s) to study response and stability.

keyPoints: Velocity is ds/dt and acceleration is dv/dt; displacement is ∫v dt.
The dot product F·d gives the work done by a constant force.
A matrix equation Ax = b represents simultaneous linear equations; eigenvalues give natural frequencies and stability.
Newton cooling dT/dt = −k(T − T∞) solves as T = T∞ + (T0 − T∞)e^(−kt).
A mass-spring-damper obeys m x″ + c x′ + kx = F(t).
The Laplace transform gives G(s) = 1/(ms² + k) for an undamped mass-spring with zero initial conditions.

en.title: Engineering drawing and computer-aided design
en.short: Orthographic views, sections, dimensioning, assembly drawings, reading drawings and CAD solid modelling.

sections.heading: Views and projection
sections.text: Orthographic projection shows a 3D object as separate 2D views, usually front, top and side. Each view looks straight at one face, so shapes keep true size where the face is parallel to the viewing plane. First-angle and third-angle projection place the views differently: in first angle the top view sits below the front view; in third angle it sits above. Visible edges are continuous lines, hidden edges dashed, and centre lines mark axes of holes. Always check the projection symbol in the title block.

sections.heading: Sections and dimensions
sections.text: A section view cuts the object with an imaginary plane and removes the near half, so internal features are seen clearly. Cut material is shown with hatching lines; parts not cut are left unhatched. Dimensioning gives each feature once: size, position and, where needed, tolerance. Use extension lines from the feature, dimension lines with arrowheads, and state the unit. A bearing bracket may need a section through its bore to show wall thickness, with the bore diameter and the height of the bore centre above the base dimensioned.

sections.heading: Assembly and reading
sections.text: An assembly drawing shows how parts fit together. It carries balloon numbers that point to a parts list, overall dimensions, and fits or clearances where they matter. It is not usually used to make each part; detail drawings do that. Reading a drawing means checking the title block, scale, units, projection symbol, views, sections, notes and revision table before judging any size. Do not scale a dimension that is not given; ask for the missing information.

sections.heading: CAD modelling
sections.text: CAD sketching starts with a 2D profile controlled by constraints and dimensions. Coincident, parallel and tangent constraints keep the shape consistent when a dimension changes. Solid modelling turns the profile into a 3D part by extrude, revolve or sweep, then adds features such as holes and rounded corners. A parametric model rebuilds when dimensions change, and the drawing is generated from it. Follow the standard adopted by your department or country.

keyPoints: Orthographic projection shows front, top and side views; first-angle puts the top view below the front view, third-angle above.
A section view uses an imaginary cut and hatching to show internal features.
Dimension each feature once, giving size, position and tolerance where needed, and state the unit.
An assembly drawing shows how parts fit and links to a parts list by balloon numbers.
Read the title block, scale, units, projection symbol and notes before using any drawing.
CAD sketching uses constraints, and solid modelling builds a parametric 3D part from a profile; follow the standard adopted by your department or country.

en.title: Statics: forces, moments and equilibrium
en.short: Force systems, moments, free-body diagrams, equilibrium, friction, centroids and simple trusses.

sections.heading: Forces and moments
sections.text: A force has magnitude, direction and application point. A force system can be replaced by a resultant: resolve forces into perpendicular components then add. The moment of a force is M = Fd, where d is the perpendicular distance to its line of action. A couple is two equal, opposite, parallel forces; its moment is M = Fd, where d is the perpendicular distance between the two forces, and this moment is the same about any point. Example: F = 50 N at d = 0.4 m gives M = 50 × 0.4 = 20 N·m.

sections.heading: Equilibrium
sections.text: A free-body diagram isolates one body and shows all external forces and moments; supports become reactions. For a particle, ΣF = 0, so ΣFx = ΣFy = 0. For a rigid body, also ΣM = 0. Example: a 4 m simply supported beam carries 200 N at 1 m from the left end. Moments about the left support: R_B × 4 = 200 × 1, so R_B = 50 N; then R_A = 150 N.

sections.heading: Friction and centroids
sections.text: Dry friction opposes relative motion between surfaces, or its tendency. Limiting static friction is Fmax = μN, where μ is the coefficient of friction and N is the normal reaction; kinetic friction is usually lower. A centroid is an area’s geometric centre. For a composite area, x̄ = ΣAx ÷ ΣA and ȳ = ΣAy ÷ ΣA. Example: a 2 m × 1 m rectangle has centroid 1 m from a short side and 0.5 m from a long side.

sections.heading: Trusses and frames
sections.text: A truss is a framework of slender members joined at pin joints, with loads at the joints. Ideal analysis assumes pin joints, joint loads, negligible member weight and two-force members. The method of joints uses particle equilibrium at each joint; the method of sections cuts the truss and uses rigid-body equilibrium. A frame has members that may carry several loads and moments, so they are not generally two-force members. Design codes differ by country; Nigeria’s COREN regulates practice.

keyPoints: Resolve forces into perpendicular components; the resultant is their vector sum.
Equilibrium of a particle needs ΣF = 0; a rigid body also needs ΣM = 0.
Moment of a force is M = Fd, and a couple has the same moment about any point.
Limiting static friction is Fmax = μN; kinetic friction is usually lower.
Centroid coordinates for a composite area are x̄ = ΣAx ÷ ΣA and ȳ = ΣAy ÷ ΣA.
Ideal trusses have pin joints, joint loads and two-force members; frames generally do not.

en.title: Dynamics: kinematics and kinetics
en.short: Particle and rigid-body plane motion, Newton’s laws, work-energy and impulse-momentum with a braking example.

sections.heading: Kinematics
sections.text:
Dynamics studies motion and its causes. Kinematics describes motion without forces. A particle is a point; a rigid body keeps its shape. In plane motion all points move in parallel planes. For constant acceleration: v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as.

On a velocity-time graph, gradient is acceleration and area is displacement. For a rotating body, a point at radius r has speed v = rω, where ω is angular velocity. Gears and pulleys can change speed and force.

sections.heading: Newton’s laws
sections.text:
Newton’s first law: a body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless a resultant force acts. The second law gives F = ma for a particle, where F is resultant force in newtons, m mass in kilograms and a acceleration in m/s².

For plane rigid-body motion, ΣF = ma, with a the acceleration of the centre of mass, and ΣM = Iα about the centre of mass, where I is moment of inertia and α angular acceleration. The third law: forces between bodies are equal and opposite.

sections.heading: Work and energy
sections.text:
Work is energy transferred by a force: W = Fd cosθ, with θ the angle between force and displacement. Kinetic energy is ½mv² and gravitational potential energy is mgh. The work-energy theorem says net work equals change in kinetic energy. Power is P = Fv.

Example: 1200 kg car at 20 m/s stops in 40 m. v² = u² + 2as gives 0 = 20² + 2a(40), so a = −5 m/s². Braking force is 1200 × 5 = 6000 N. Time is 20 ÷ 5 = 4 s.

sections.heading: Impulse and momentum
sections.text:
Linear momentum is p = mv. Impulse is J = FΔt for a constant force, or ∫F dt in general, and equals change in momentum.

If no external impulse acts along a line, total momentum is conserved: m1u1 + m2u2 = m1v1 + m2v2. This applies to collisions and impacts. Check units: N·s equals kg·m/s. Longer stopping time for the same momentum change means smaller force.

keyPoints: Constant acceleration: v = u + at, s = ut + ½at² and v² = u² + 2as.
On a velocity-time graph, gradient is acceleration and area is displacement.
Newton’s second law for a particle is F = ma; for plane rigid-body motion use ΣF = ma and ΣM = Iα about the centre of mass.
Work-energy theorem: net work equals change in kinetic energy, and power is P = Fv.
Impulse equals change in momentum: J = FΔt = Δ(mv).
In SI units, N·s equals kg·m/s; check units before calculating.

en.title: Materials science for engineers
en.short: Atomic bonding, crystal structure, defects, phase diagrams, testing and the main material families.

sections.heading: Bonding and crystals
sections.text:
Atoms bond by ionic, covalent, metallic or weak van der Waals forces. Bond type controls stiffness, melting point and conductivity. Metals have delocalised electrons, so they conduct and deform. Ceramics have strong ionic or covalent bonds, so they are hard and brittle. Polymers are long chain molecules held by covalent bonds and weak forces between chains.

Crystals repeat a unit cell. Common metal structures are body-centred cubic (BCC), face-centred cubic (FCC) and hexagonal close-packed (HCP). Density ρ = nA ÷ (N_A V), where n is atoms per cell, A is atomic mass, N_A is Avogadro’s number and V is cell volume.

sections.heading: Defects and phases
sections.text: Real crystals contain defects. Point defects include vacancies. Dislocations are line defects; their motion causes plastic deformation. Grain boundaries hinder dislocation motion, so smaller grains usually raise strength. Phase diagrams plot phases against temperature and composition. The lever rule gives phase fractions in a two-phase region. Alloying and heat treatment change microstructure and properties.

sections.heading: Testing and properties
sections.text:
A tensile test records force and extension. Engineering stress is σ = F ÷ A₀; strain is ε = ΔL ÷ L₀. The initial slope gives Young’s modulus E = σ ÷ ε. Yield strength starts plastic strain; ultimate tensile strength is the maximum stress; ductility is strain at fracture. Hardness and impact tests measure indentation resistance and sudden loading.

Example: 10 mm diameter gives A₀ = π × 10² ÷ 4 = 78.54 mm². At F = 15.7 kN, σ = 15,700 ÷ 78.54 = 199.9 N/mm². At L₀ = 50 mm, 0.05 mm extension gives ε = 0.001 and E = 199.9 ÷ 0.001 = 199,900 N/mm², about 200 GPa.

sections.heading: Material families
sections.text: Metals are strong, ductile and conductive. Polymers are light, easy to shape and often viscoelastic, so their response depends on time and temperature. Ceramics are hard, wear resistant and brittle. Composites combine two materials, such as stiff fibres in a polymer matrix, to give properties neither has alone. Material standards differ by country; check the current national standard.

keyPoints: Atomic bonding and crystal structure set the basic stiffness, melting point and conductivity of a material.
Dislocations, vacancies and grain boundaries control plastic deformation and strength.
Phase diagrams show which phases exist at a given temperature and composition; the lever rule gives their fractions.
Engineering stress σ = F ÷ A₀ and strain ε = ΔL ÷ L₀; Young’s modulus E = σ ÷ ε in the elastic region.
Metals are ductile and conductive, polymers are light and viscoelastic, ceramics are hard and brittle, and composites combine properties.
Material standards and design codes differ by country, so check the current national standard.

en.title: Mechanics of materials: stress, strain and axial loading
en.short: Normal and shear stress, strain, Hooke’s law, axial deformation, thermal stress and pressure vessels.

sections.heading: Stress and strain
sections.text: Normal stress is force perpendicular to area: σ = F ÷ A, in N/m² (Pa) or N/mm² (MPa). Shear stress acts parallel to area: τ = V ÷ A, where V is the shear force. Strain is deformation per original length: ε = ΔL ÷ L, dimensionless. It can be tensile or compressive. A stress is not a force; it describes how concentrated a force is.

sections.heading: Elastic constants
sections.text: Hooke’s law for a linear elastic material is σ = Eε, where E is Young’s modulus. The shear form is τ = Gγ, with G the shear modulus and γ the shear strain (change in angle). Poisson’s ratio ν = −lateral strain ÷ axial strain. For an isotropic material, G = E ÷ [2(1 + ν)]. Bulk modulus K relates pressure to volume change. These constants are material properties, not design limits. Yielding and failure depend on the material and the design code, which differs by country; check the code that applies.

sections.heading: Axial deformation
sections.text:
A bar of length L, area A and modulus E under axial force F stretches by δ = FL ÷ (AE). Use consistent units, for example N and mm. The same formula gives shortening under compression. Stiffness is F ÷ δ = AE ÷ L.

Example: a steel bar 20 mm diameter, 2 m long, F = 50 kN, E = 200 GPa.
A = π × 20² ÷ 4 = 314.2 mm²
δ = 50,000 × 2,000 ÷ (314.2 × 200,000) = 1.59 mm
σ = 50,000 ÷ 314.2 = 159 N/mm²

sections.heading: Thermal, concentration, vessels
sections.text: A fully restrained bar heated by ΔT develops thermal stress σ = EαΔT, where α is the coefficient of thermal expansion; it is compressive when expansion is prevented. A stress concentration raises local stress near holes, notches or sudden changes: Kt = σmax ÷ σnom. Kt depends on geometry, not material. In a thin-walled cylinder under internal pressure p, radius r and wall thickness t (t much smaller than r), hoop (circumferential) stress is σ = pr ÷ t and longitudinal stress is σ = pr ÷ (2t). A sphere has σ = pr ÷ (2t).

keyPoints: Normal stress is σ = F ÷ A and shear stress is τ = V ÷ A; strain is ε = ΔL ÷ L.
Hooke’s law is σ = Eε in tension and τ = Gγ in shear; for isotropic materials G = E ÷ [2(1 + ν)].
Axial deformation is δ = FL ÷ (AE), using consistent units such as N and mm.
Fully restrained thermal stress is σ = EαΔT; stress concentration is Kt = σmax ÷ σnom.
Thin-walled cylinder stresses are hoop pr ÷ t and longitudinal pr ÷ (2t); a sphere has pr ÷ (2t).
Elastic constants and allowable stresses depend on the material, and design codes and registration differ by country, for example COREN in Nigeria.

en.title: Engineering thermodynamics: properties and laws
en.short: Systems and properties, work and heat, the first and second laws, entropy, ideal gases and simple cycles.

sections.heading: Systems and properties
sections.text:
A thermodynamic system is the matter or region you study; everything outside it is the surroundings. A closed system keeps a fixed mass, though energy can cross its boundary. An open system, or control volume, lets mass cross. An isolated system lets neither mass nor energy cross.

A property is a quantity that depends only on the state, such as temperature, pressure, volume and internal energy. Intensive properties (temperature, pressure) do not depend on size; extensive ones (volume, mass, internal energy) do. For a simple compressible substance, two independent intensive properties fix the state.

sections.heading: Work, heat and the first law
sections.text:
Work is energy transfer through a force acting over a distance; boundary work in a cylinder is W = ∫p dV. Heat is energy transfer driven by a temperature difference. Both are path functions: they depend on how a change is made, not only on the end states.

The first law for a closed system is Q − W = ΔU, with Q positive into the system and W positive out of it. For steady flow through an open system, q − w = Δh + Δke + Δpe.

Example: a gas takes in 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work.
ΔU = 500 − 200 = 300 J

sections.heading: Second law and entropy
sections.text:
The second law says heat flows by itself from hot to cold, and no device running in a cycle converts all its heat input into work. The Kelvin-Planck and Clausius statements express this. A reversible process gives the most work and needs the least work input.

Entropy S is a property. For a reversible process ΔS = ∫dQ ÷ T, and for an isolated system ΔS ≥ 0. Real processes create entropy. A Carnot engine working between hot and cold reservoirs at absolute temperatures Th and Tc has efficiency η = 1 − Tc ÷ Th.

sections.heading: Ideal gases and simple cycles
sections.text:
An ideal gas obeys pV = mRT, where R is the gas constant for that gas, R = Ru ÷ M. For air, R = 287 J/(kg·K). Also cp − cv = R and γ = cp ÷ cv.

Example: 1 kg of air at 300 K and 100 kPa.
V = mRT ÷ p = (1 × 287 × 300) ÷ 100,000 = 0.861 m³

A power cycle takes heat at high temperature, rejects heat at low temperature and delivers net work, so η = Wnet ÷ Qin. A refrigerator or heat pump uses work to move heat from cold to warm. COP is the wanted heat transfer divided by the work input: Qcold ÷ W for a refrigerator, Qhot ÷ W for a heat pump. Cycle analysis comes later.

keyPoints: First law for a closed system: Q − W = ΔU, with Q in and W out taken as positive.
Boundary work is W = ∫p dV; heat and work are path functions, not properties.
Second law: for an isolated system ΔS ≥ 0, and no cyclic device converts all heat to work.
Carnot efficiency is η = 1 − Tc ÷ Th, using absolute temperatures.
Ideal gas law: pV = mRT, with cp − cv = R and γ = cp ÷ cv.
Power cycle efficiency is η = Wnet ÷ Qin; COP is Qcold ÷ W for a refrigerator and Qhot ÷ W for a heat pump.

en.title: Fluid mechanics: properties and hydrostatics
en.short: Fluid properties, pressure, manometry, forces on surfaces, buoyancy and simple flow equations.

sections.heading: Fluid properties
sections.text: Density ρ is mass per volume. Specific weight is γ = ρg. Dynamic viscosity μ measures resistance to shear; kinematic viscosity is ν = μ ÷ ρ. Pressure is force per area, p = F ÷ A. Absolute pressure is measured from vacuum; gauge pressure from local atmospheric pressure. In a static fluid, p = p0 + ρgh, where h is depth and p0 is surface pressure. Pressure acts equally in all directions at a point (Pascal’s law).

sections.heading: Manometry and surfaces
sections.text:
A manometer uses a liquid column to measure pressure; a column of height h adds ρgh at its base. For a plane surface, hydrostatic force is F = ρ g h_c A, where h_c is the vertical depth to the centroid and A is area. For a vertical surface, centre of pressure is h_cp = h_c + I_c ÷ (A h_c), where I_c is the second moment of area about the centroid.

Example: a vertical rectangular gate 2 m wide and 3 m high has its top at the water surface. h_c = 1.5 m, A = 6 m². F = 1000 × 9.81 × 1.5 × 6 = 88,290 N ≈ 88.3 kN. I_c = 2 × 3³ ÷ 12 = 4.5 m⁴, so h_cp = 1.5 + 4.5 ÷ (6 × 1.5) = 2.0 m.

sections.heading: Buoyancy
sections.text: Archimedes’ principle says the buoyant force equals the weight of fluid displaced. A floating body displaces its own weight. Stability depends on the centre of gravity and centre of buoyancy; metacentric height measures initial stability.

sections.heading: Flow equations
sections.text: For steady incompressible flow, continuity gives A1v1 = A2v2. Bernoulli’s equation along a streamline, with no losses, is p ÷ (ρg) + v² ÷ (2g) + z = constant. The momentum equation for a control volume is ΣF = ρQ(v_out − v_in), where Q is volume flow rate. These solve simple pipe and nozzle problems.

keyPoints: Density is mass per volume; specific weight is γ = ρg and kinematic viscosity is ν = μ ÷ ρ.
Hydrostatic pressure at depth h is p = p0 + ρgh; gauge pressure is measured from atmospheric pressure.
Hydrostatic force on a plane surface is F = ρ g h_c A, with centre of pressure h_cp = h_c + I_c ÷ (A h_c) for a vertical surface.
Buoyant force equals the weight of displaced fluid (Archimedes’ principle).
Continuity for incompressible flow: A1v1 = A2v2.
Bernoulli along a streamline: p ÷ (ρg) + v² ÷ (2g) + z = constant; momentum: ΣF = ρQ(v_out − v_in).

en.title: Electrical and electronic principles for mechanical engineers
en.short: DC and AC circuits, magnetic circuits, transformers, motors, sensors and power electronics for mechanical systems.

sections.heading: DC circuits
sections.text:
Direct current (DC) flows one way. Ohm’s law relates voltage V, current I and resistance R: V = I R. In series, resistances add; in parallel, 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2. Kirchhoff’s laws state that current into a node equals current out, and voltages around a loop sum to zero. Power is P = V I = I² R = V²/R.

Example: a 12 V supply across 4 Ω and 8 Ω in series. Total R = 12 Ω, so I = 12 ÷ 12 = 1 A. The drops are 4 V and 8 V, and total power is 12 V × 1 A = 12 W.

sections.heading: AC and magnetism
sections.text: Alternating current (AC) reverses periodically; its RMS value gives the equivalent heating effect. Capacitors and inductors oppose change, giving reactance, and impedance Z combines resistance and reactance. In magnetic circuits, flux Φ is driven by magnetomotive force F = N I through reluctance S = l ÷ (μ A), where μ is permeability. This mirrors Ohm’s law: Φ = F ÷ S. Magnetic flux density is B = Φ ÷ A.

sections.heading: Transformers and machines
sections.text: A transformer changes AC voltage by the turns ratio: V1 ÷ V2 = N1 ÷ N2. It transfers power by mutual induction, with small losses. Electric motors convert electrical energy to rotation; generators do the reverse. Both rely on the force on a current in a magnetic field and on induced emf. Mechanical engineers specify torque, speed and duty, and must allow for starting current and cooling.

sections.heading: Sensors and drives
sections.text: Sensors turn physical quantities into electrical signals: thermocouples and resistance temperature detectors for temperature, strain gauges for force, encoders for position. Power electronics switch and control power. Diodes rectify, thyristors and transistors (MOSFETs, IGBTs) switch, and pulse-width modulation (PWM) varies average voltage. Variable-speed drives use these to match motor speed to load. Wiring rules and component ratings differ by country and application; follow the current national code and manufacturer data.

keyPoints: Ohm’s law is V = I R; series resistances add and parallel conductances add.
DC power is P = V I = I² R = V²/R.
A magnetic circuit follows Φ = F ÷ S, with F = N I and S = l ÷ (μ A).
A transformer obeys V1 ÷ V2 = N1 ÷ N2 and transfers power by mutual induction.
Motors and generators convert between electrical and mechanical energy through magnetic fields.
Sensors and power electronics, including PWM variable-speed drives, connect mechanical systems to electrical control.

en.title: Engineering computing and numerical methods
en.short: Programming basics and numerical methods for roots, equations, interpolation, calculus and ODEs, with error checks.

sections.heading: Programming basics
sections.text:
A program is a list of instructions. It covers variables, data types, arrays, loops, conditionals and functions. An algorithm is a finite procedure that solves a problem; pseudocode states it without depending on one language.

Computers store numbers with finite precision, so floating-point arithmetic causes round-off error. Truncation error comes from replacing an exact process by an approximation, such as a finite series. Test code on cases with known answers before trusting it.

sections.heading: Roots and linear equations
sections.text:
Root finding solves f(x)=0. Bisection keeps a bracket where f changes sign and halves it repeatedly: safe but slow. Newton-Raphson uses x_new = x − f(x) ÷ f'(x). It is fast near a root but needs the derivative and a good start.

Example: solve x² − 2 = 0 from x = 1.5. f = 0.25, f' = 3, so x_new = 1.5 − 0.25 ÷ 3 = 1.4167. Squaring gives about 2.007, closer to 2.

Linear systems Ax = b are solved by Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting, which swaps rows so the pivot is the largest remaining coefficient in its column in magnitude, to limit round-off error. Substitute the answer back and compute the residual b − Ax.

sections.heading: Interpolation and calculus
sections.text:
Interpolation estimates values between known points. Linear interpolation between (x0,y0) and (x1,y1) gives y = y0 + (x − x0)(y1 − y0) ÷ (x1 − x0). High-degree polynomials can oscillate; splines use piecewise low-degree curves.

Numerical integration sums areas. The trapezium rule is ∫ f dx ≈ h/2 [f0 + 2f1 + ... + 2f(n−1) + fn]. Numerical differentiation uses finite differences, for example f'(x) ≈ [f(x+h) − f(x−h)] ÷ (2h). A smaller h reduces truncation error but increases round-off.

sections.heading: ODEs and checking
sections.text:
An ordinary differential equation (ODE) contains one independent variable and derivatives. For y' = f(x,y), Euler’s method steps y_{n+1} = y_n + h f(x_n,y_n). It is simple but needs small h. Runge-Kutta methods are more accurate.

Always check numerical work: substitute back, refine the step, compare with an exact solution where one exists, and watch residuals and convergence. Report error estimates; a single unchecked run is not evidence.

keyPoints: Store and calculate in consistent units, and test programs on cases with known answers.
Newton-Raphson: x_new = x − f(x) ÷ f'(x); it is fast near a root but can fail from a poor start.
The trapezium rule is ∫ f dx ≈ h/2 [f0 + 2f1 + ... + 2f(n−1) + fn].
Central difference: f'(x) ≈ [f(x+h) − f(x−h)] ÷ (2h); small h trades truncation error for round-off.
Euler’s method: y_{n+1} = y_n + h f(x_n,y_n).
Check every result by substitution, residual, step refinement or comparison with an exact solution.

en.title: Mechanics of materials: beams, torsion and deflection
en.short: Shear and moment diagrams, bending and shear stress, shaft torsion, deflection, buckling and combined loading.

sections.heading: Diagrams
sections.text: Draw the shear force diagram (SFD) and bending moment diagram (BMD) first. For a beam with distributed load w, dV/dx = −w and dM/dx = V, so the change in shear between two points equals the area under the load diagram and the change in moment equals the area under the shear diagram. A point load makes the shear jump and the moment change slope; a couple makes the moment jump. Maximum bending stress occurs where the bending moment is largest, not where shear is largest.

sections.heading: Bending and shear
sections.text:
For a linear elastic, homogeneous beam with small deflection and no axial load, M ÷ I = σ ÷ y = E ÷ R. I is the second moment of area about the neutral axis, y the distance from it, R the radius of curvature. Shear stress is τ = VQ ÷ (Ib), where Q is the first moment of the area beyond the level and b the width of the section there. In a rectangle τmax = 1.5V ÷ A.
Example: b = 100 mm, d = 200 mm, M = 20 kN·m, V = 30 kN.
Z, the section modulus, is bd² ÷ 6 = 100 × 200² ÷ 6 = 666,667 mm³
σ = 20 × 10⁶ ÷ 666,667 = 30 N/mm²
τmax = 1.5 × 30,000 ÷ 20,000 = 2.25 N/mm²

sections.heading: Torsion and deflection
sections.text: Circular shafts: T ÷ J = τ ÷ r = Gθ ÷ L, where J is the polar second moment of area; J = πd⁴ ÷ 32 for a solid shaft. For a simply supported beam under a uniform load w per unit length, δ = 5wL⁴ ÷ (384EI) at mid-span. These formulas assume elastic material, small strain, prismatic section and no buckling. Deflection limits come from national codes; check the current code for your country.

sections.heading: Buckling and combined
sections.text: Euler buckling: Pcr = π²EI ÷ (KL)², where K depends on end conditions. It assumes an elastic, straight, centrally loaded column; real columns need imperfection and code checks. Under combined loading, add stresses at the same point only if the response is linear and deflections are small. Otherwise use interaction equations or analysis.

keyPoints: Shear force and bending moment are linked by dM/dx = V and dV/dx = −w.
Bending equation: M ÷ I = σ ÷ y = E ÷ R; for a rectangle the section modulus Z = bd² ÷ 6.
Shear stress: τ = VQ ÷ (Ib); in a rectangle τmax = 1.5V ÷ A.
Torsion: T ÷ J = τ ÷ r = Gθ ÷ L; for a solid shaft J = πd⁴ ÷ 32.
Mid-span deflection of a simply supported beam under a uniform load w per unit length: δ = 5wL⁴ ÷ (384EI).
Euler buckling load: Pcr = π²EI ÷ (KL)², valid only for elastic slender columns.

en.title: Machine elements and mechanisms
en.short: Gears, drives, shafts, couplings, clutches, brakes, bearings, springs, linkages and cams, with sizing.

sections.heading: Gears and drives
sections.text:
Gears transmit motion by teeth. Module m = d ÷ z, where d is pitch diameter and z is tooth number. For a pair, speed ratio (driver speed ÷ driven speed) = z2 ÷ z1 and centre distance = (d1 + d2) ÷ 2.

Belts and chains are flexible drives; belts suit long centres, chains give positive timing. Approximate open belt length L = 2C + π(D1 + D2) ÷ 2 + (D2 − D1)² ÷ (4C), where C is centre distance. Use manufacturer power and service ratings.

sections.heading: Shafts and contact elements
sections.text:
A shaft carries torque T and bending. For a solid circular shaft, τ = T r ÷ J with J = πd⁴ ÷ 32, so d³ = 16T ÷ (πτallow). Power P = Tω, with ω in rad/s.

Flexible couplings join shafts and tolerate some misalignment. Clutches connect under load; brakes absorb energy. Friction torque depends on clamp force, friction coefficient and mean radius. Bearings support shafts; rolling bearing life L10 = (C ÷ P)^p million revolutions, where C is the basic dynamic load rating and P is the equivalent radial load, with p = 3 for ball and 10 ÷ 3 for roller bearings. Springs have stiffness k = F ÷ δ and energy Fδ ÷ 2.

sections.heading: Mechanisms and example
sections.text:
Linkages and cams convert motion. Planar linkage mobility with lower pairs only is M = 3(n − 1) − 2j, where n is the number of links and j is the number of lower pairs (pin and slider joints). Cam followers need checking for pressure angle and contact stress.

Example: a 20-tooth pinion drives a 60-tooth gear, module 3 mm, pinion speed 1200 rpm. Ratio = 60 ÷ 20 = 3, so gear speed = 400 rpm. Pitch diameters are 3 × 20 = 60 mm and 3 × 60 = 180 mm; centre distance = (60 + 180) ÷ 2 = 120 mm. Design standards and professional registration differ by country, for example COREN in Nigeria; check current standards and manufacturer catalogues.

keyPoints: Gear module m = d ÷ z; for a pair, speed ratio (driver speed ÷ driven speed) = z2 ÷ z1 and centre distance = (d1 + d2) ÷ 2.
Approximate open belt length: L = 2C + π(D1 + D2) ÷ 2 + (D2 − D1)² ÷ (4C).
Solid shaft under torque: d³ = 16T ÷ (πτallow), and power P = Tω with ω in rad/s.

Rolling bearing basic rating life: L10 = (C ÷ P)^p million revolutions, where C is the basic dynamic load rating and P is the equivalent radial load; p = 3 for ball bearings and 10 ÷ 3 for roller bearings.
Spring stiffness k = F ÷ δ and stored energy = Fδ ÷ 2.
Planar linkage mobility M = 3(n − 1) − 2j; check cams for pressure angle and contact stress, and use current manufacturer data and national standards.

en.title: Manufacturing processes
en.short: Casting, forming, machining, joining, additive and CNC, with defects and process selection.

sections.heading: Casting and forming
sections.text: Casting pours molten metal into a mould. Solidification time follows Chvorinov’s rule: t = B (V/A)², where V is volume, A is cooling surface area and B is a mould constant. A large V/A means slow cooling, so a riser feeds shrinkage. Forming shapes metal by plastic deformation: rolling, forging, extrusion. Hot working needs less force because the metal is weaker when hot; cold working gives a better finish and higher strength but needs more force. Material choice matters: castability for casting, ductility for forming.

sections.heading: Machining and joining
sections.text:
Machining removes material with a cutting tool: turning, milling, drilling. It holds tight tolerances and fine finishes, but cost rises as tolerance tightens. Joining covers welding, brazing, soldering, adhesives and fasteners. Weldability depends on the material.

Example: turning a 50 mm bar at 200 m/min, feed 0.2 mm/rev, depth 2 mm. Spindle speed N = 200,000 ÷ (π × 50) = 1273 rev/min. Material removal rate = π × 50 × 2 × 0.2 × 1273 ≈ 80,000 mm³/min.

sections.heading: Additive and CNC
sections.text: Additive manufacturing builds parts layer by layer from a digital model, for example powder bed fusion or material extrusion. It suits complex shapes and small batches but is slow and limited in size. CNC production uses computer-controlled machine tools that follow a program, giving repeatable parts with less operator skill. Both depend on the material: powder flow, melt behaviour, tool wear.

sections.heading: Defects and selection
sections.text: Common defects: casting has porosity and shrinkage; forming has cracking and springback; machining has chatter and poor finish; welding has porosity and lack of fusion; additive has residual stress and rough surfaces. Process selection weighs quantity, material, tolerance, surface finish and cost. Tight tolerances usually mean machining after another process. Design codes and tolerance standards differ by country; check the current national standard.

keyPoints: Chvorinov’s rule: solidification time t = B (V/A)².
Tighter tolerances raise cost; specify only what the function needs.
Casting suits complex shapes; forming suits ductile metals in bulk.
Welding defects include porosity and lack of fusion.
Additive manufacturing suits complex, low-volume parts but is slow.
Process selection depends on quantity, material, tolerance, finish and cost.

en.title: Engineering metrology and measurement
en.short: Instruments, errors, calibration, tolerances, fits, surface finish and uncertainty in inspection.

sections.heading: Instruments and errors
sections.text:
Metrology is the science of measurement. Instruments include vernier caliper, micrometer, dial gauge, gauge blocks, coordinate measuring machine (CMM) and roughness tester. Resolution is the smallest indicated change; accuracy is closeness to true value; repeatability is closeness of repeated readings.

Errors are systematic (zero error, calibration, temperature), random (vibration, reading variation) or gross (mistakes). Thermal error: a 100 mm steel part at 25 °C, measured against a 20 °C standard, with α = 0.0000115 /K, expands by 100 × 0.0000115 × 5 = 0.00575 mm.

sections.heading: Calibration and uncertainty
sections.text:
Calibration compares an instrument with a traceable standard and records corrections. Traceability is an unbroken chain to a national or international standard. Uncertainty is a range likely to contain the true value; it is not error. Expanded uncertainty U = k u_c, where u_c is combined standard uncertainty; k = 2 gives about 95 % coverage.

Uncertainty affects acceptance. For 10.00 ± 0.02 mm, a reading of 10.018 mm is inside. If U = 0.005 mm, it is within U of the upper limit, so acceptance is uncertain. Use a guard band, meaning accept only readings safely inside the limit, or re-measure.

sections.heading: Tolerances and fits
sections.text:
Tolerance is the allowed difference between upper and lower limits. A clearance fit leaves a gap; an interference fit overlaps; a transition fit may do either. Hole-basis and shaft-basis systems are common; ISO 286 defines letter and grade systems, but national practice and codes vary.

Example: hole 20.000 to 20.021 mm, shaft 19.980 to 19.993 mm.
Maximum clearance = 20.021 − 19.980 = 0.041 mm.
Minimum clearance = 20.000 − 19.993 = 0.007 mm.
This is a clearance fit.

sections.heading: Surface finish and inspection
sections.text: Surface finish describes small-scale texture. Ra is the arithmetic mean deviation of the profile from its mean line; lower Ra is smoother. Inspection uses go/no-go gauges, CMMs and sampling plans. Gauge repeatability and reproducibility (gauge R&R) studies estimate measurement variation. Set calibration intervals and acceptance rules from uncertainty and risk.

keyPoints: Accuracy is closeness to the true value; repeatability is closeness of repeated readings.
Calibration corrects systematic errors; repeated readings and good technique reduce random errors.
Thermal expansion error is ΔL = L α ΔT; check temperature when measuring to tight tolerances.
Expanded uncertainty is U = k u_c; k = 2 gives about 95 % coverage.
Acceptance near a tolerance limit needs a guard band, because a reading inside the limit may still be uncertain.
Tolerance is the difference between upper and lower limits; clearance, interference and transition fits describe assembly.

en.title: Mechanical vibrations
en.short: Free and forced vibration, damping, resonance, transmissibility, isolation, balancing and MDOF systems.

sections.heading: Free vibration and damping
sections.text:
Free vibration of a single-degree-of-freedom (SDOF) system is one mass m on a spring k. Without damping, ωn = √(k/m) rad/s and x = A cos(ωn t) + B sin(ωn t). Damping c opposes velocity. The damping ratio is ζ = c ÷ cc, where critical damping cc = 2√(km). ζ < 1 is underdamped (oscillates and decays), ζ = 1 critical, ζ > 1 overdamped.

The damped frequency is ωd = ωn√(1 − ζ²). Example: m = 10 kg, k = 4000 N/m, c = 40 N·s/m. ωn = √(4000 ÷ 10) = 20 rad/s, fn = 3.18 Hz. cc = 2√(4000 × 10) = 400 N·s/m, so ζ = 0.1.

sections.heading: Forced vibration and resonance
sections.text:
Harmonic force F0 sin ωt gives steady amplitude X = (F0/k) ÷ √((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²), with r = ω/ωn. Resonance is r near 1, where X peaks; at r = 1, X = F0 ÷ (2ζk). Damping limits the peak.

Example: F0 = 50 N, k = 4000 N/m, ζ = 0.1, r = 1: X = 50 ÷ (2 × 0.1 × 4000) = 0.0625 m = 62.5 mm. Phase lag grows through resonance.

sections.heading: Transmissibility and isolation
sections.text:
Transmissibility TR is the ratio of transmitted force (or motion) to the applied force (or base motion). For force: TR = √((1 + (2ζr)²) ÷ ((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²)). Isolation needs r > √2, where TR < 1.

Example: r = 3, ζ = 0.1: numerator 1 + 0.36 = 1.36; denominator 64 + 0.36 = 64.36; TR = √(1.36 ÷ 64.36) = 0.145, so 14.5% is transmitted. Soft springs or added mass lower ωn and raise r.

sections.heading: Balancing and MDOF systems
sections.text:
Balancing reduces rotating unbalance. Static balancing puts the centre of mass on the axis using one correction mass. Dynamic balancing uses two planes to cancel the couple from a distributed unbalance.

A multi-degree-of-freedom (MDOF) system has several masses or coordinates; it has as many natural frequencies as degrees of freedom, each with a mode shape. Real machines respond in combinations of these modes, so modal analysis is used.

keyPoints: For an SDOF system, ωn = √(k/m) and the damping ratio is ζ = c ÷ (2√(km)).
Underdamped systems (ζ < 1) oscillate at ωd = ωn√(1 − ζ²) and decay.
Steady-state amplitude is X = (F0/k) ÷ √((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²), with r = ω/ωn; resonance occurs near r = 1.
Force transmissibility is TR = √((1 + (2ζr)²) ÷ ((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²)); isolation needs r > √2.
Balancing corrects static unbalance with one mass and dynamic unbalance with two planes.
An MDOF system has as many natural frequencies and mode shapes as degrees of freedom.

en.title: Heat transfer: conduction, convection, radiation and exchangers
en.short: Conduction, convection, radiation, fins, lumped capacitance and heat exchanger design.

sections.heading: Conduction and fins
sections.text: Conduction is heat flow through a material without bulk motion. Fourier’s law is Q = kA ΔT ÷ L, where k is thermal conductivity in W/(m·K), A area and L thickness. A plane wall has resistance R = L ÷ (kA), so Q = ΔT ÷ R. Fins add area. Fin efficiency η is actual heat transfer divided by the ideal if the whole fin were at base temperature; it falls as the fin lengthens. Fins help when the surface coefficient is low.

sections.heading: Convection and coefficients
sections.text: Convection is heat transfer between a solid surface and a moving fluid. Newton’s law is Q = hA(Ts − T∞), where h is the heat transfer coefficient in W/(m²·K). h depends on fluid, velocity, geometry and flow regime, so it comes from correlations or experiment. For a plane wall, 1 ÷ U = 1 ÷ h1 + L ÷ k + 1 ÷ h2. Example: A = 2 m², L = 0.1 m, k = 0.5 W/(m·K), h1 = 10, h2 = 20 W/(m²·K), ΔT = 80 K. Then 1 ÷ U = 0.35, U = 2.86 W/(m²·K), Q = 458 W.

sections.heading: Radiation
sections.text: Radiation is heat transfer by electromagnetic waves; it needs no medium. A real surface emits Q = εσA T⁴, where ε is emissivity (0 to 1), σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W/(m²·K⁴) and T is absolute temperature. Net exchange with surroundings at Tsur is Q = εσA(Ts⁴ − Tsur⁴). It matters most at high temperature.

sections.heading: Lumped capacitance and exchangers
sections.text: Lumped capacitance treats a body as one temperature. It is valid when Bi = hLc ÷ k is small, often below 0.1; Lc is volume divided by surface area. Then T(t) − T∞ = (T0 − T∞) exp(−t ÷ τ), with τ = ρVc ÷ (hA), where ρ is density and c is specific heat capacity. Heat exchangers transfer heat between fluids. For a simple exchanger, Q = U A ΔTlm, where ΔTlm is the log-mean temperature difference, (ΔT1 − ΔT2) ÷ ln(ΔT1 ÷ ΔT2), with ΔT1 and ΔT2 the temperature differences at the two ends; counterflow gives the highest ΔTlm. Other arrangements use a correction factor F.

keyPoints: Fourier’s law: Q = kA ΔT ÷ L; plane-wall resistance is L ÷ (kA).
Newton’s law: Q = hA(Ts − T∞); h depends on flow and geometry.
Overall coefficient: 1 ÷ U = 1 ÷ h1 + L ÷ k + 1 ÷ h2 for a plane wall.
Fin efficiency η is actual heat transfer divided by the ideal whole-fin value.
Radiation: Q = εσA(Ts⁴ − Tsur⁴), with σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W/(m²·K⁴).
Lumped capacitance needs small Bi = hLc ÷ k; heat exchangers use Q = U A ΔTlm.

en.title: Applied thermodynamics and power cycles
en.short: Rankine, Brayton, Otto and Diesel cycles, combustion, efficiency and engines.

sections.heading: Steam cycles
sections.text: The Rankine cycle is the ideal steam power cycle: pump, boiler, turbine, condenser. Water is pumped as liquid, boiled at constant pressure, expanded, then condensed. Steam tables give enthalpy h at each state. η = (Wturbine − Wpump) ÷ Qin = ((h1 − h2) − (h4 − h3)) ÷ (h1 − h4). Example: h1 = 3,200, h2 = 2,200, h3 = 200, h4 = 210 kJ/kg. η = (1,000 − 10) ÷ (3,200 − 210) = 990 ÷ 2,990 = 0.331, about 33%. Real cycles add losses.

sections.heading: Gas cycles
sections.text: The Brayton cycle is the ideal gas turbine cycle: compressor, heater or combustion chamber, turbine. For constant specific heat, η = 1 − 1 ÷ rp^((γ−1)/γ), where rp is pressure ratio and γ = cp/cv. Higher rp raises efficiency, but turbine inlet temperature limits it. Example: rp = 10, γ = 1.4. 10^0.2857 = 1.931; η = 1 − 1 ÷ 1.931 = 0.482, about 48%. Real turbines use isentropic efficiencies, which compare real work with the ideal constant-entropy work, and blade cooling.

sections.heading: Reciprocating engines
sections.text: The Otto cycle models the spark-ignition engine: two isentropic and two constant-volume processes, with η = 1 − 1 ÷ r^(γ−1), where r is the compression ratio (a volume ratio). The Diesel cycle models the compression-ignition engine: heat addition is at constant pressure, so η = 1 − (1 ÷ r^(γ−1)) × (ρ^γ − 1) ÷ (γ(ρ − 1)), where ρ is the cut-off ratio, the volume at the end of heat addition divided by the volume at the start. Example: Otto with r = 8, γ = 1.4: η = 1 − 1 ÷ 8^0.4 = 1 − 1 ÷ 2.297 = 0.565, about 56%. Real engines lose efficiency through friction and heat loss.

sections.heading: Combustion and efficiency
sections.text: Combustion releases heat by oxidising fuel. The stoichiometric air-fuel ratio is the minimum air for complete combustion; excess air improves mixing but lowers flame temperature. Efficiency is useful work ÷ heat supplied. Specific fuel consumption, the fuel used per unit of work output, compares engines. Property tables give enthalpy and entropy; use them rather than guessed values. Emissions rules vary by country and engine type, so check current local regulations.

keyPoints: Rankine efficiency is η = ((h1 − h2) − (h4 − h3)) ÷ (h1 − h4), using steam-table enthalpies.
Ideal Brayton efficiency is η = 1 − 1 ÷ rp^((γ−1)/γ), where rp is pressure ratio.
Ideal Otto efficiency is η = 1 − 1 ÷ r^(γ−1), where r is the compression ratio (a volume ratio).
Ideal Diesel efficiency is η = 1 − (1 ÷ r^(γ−1)) × (ρ^γ − 1) ÷ (γ(ρ − 1)), where ρ is cut-off ratio.
Combustion needs at least the stoichiometric air-fuel ratio; excess air lowers flame temperature.
Property tables and isentropic efficiencies make cycle calculations realistic; emissions rules vary by country.

en.title: Fluid machinery and pipe systems
en.short: Pipe losses, networks, pump and system curves, cavitation, similarity and machine selection.

sections.heading: Pipe flow losses
sections.text:
Friction head loss is h_f = f (L/D)(V²/2g); f is the Darcy friction factor, L and D length and diameter, V velocity, g gravity. f depends on Reynolds number Re = ρVD/μ and relative roughness ε/D. Minor losses are h_m = K V²/2g, K the loss coefficient.

Example: D = 0.1 m, L = 100 m, V = 2 m/s, f = 0.02, K = 5. V²/2g = 0.204 m. h_f = 0.02 × 1000 × 0.204 = 4.08 m. h_m = 5 × 0.204 = 1.02 m. Total = 5.10 m.

sections.heading: Networks and operating point
sections.text:
Pipes in series carry the same flow and their losses add. Pipes in parallel have the same head loss and their flows add. Networks need continuity at junctions and energy around loops.

The system curve is h_sys = h_static + R Q², where h_static is static lift and R resistance. The pump curve plots head against Q. Their intersection is the operating point; choose a pump near its best efficiency point.

sections.heading: Pumps, fans, turbines
sections.text: A pump adds head H = (p₂ − p₁)/(ρg) + (z₂ − z₁) + (V₂² − V₁²)/(2g). Fans are low-pressure gas movers; turbines extract head and drive generators. Cavitation occurs when local pressure falls below vapour pressure, forming bubbles that collapse and damage surfaces. Net positive suction head available (NPSH_A) must exceed the pump’s required NPSH; NPSH_A falls with suction lift and rising temperature. Maker data give the required NPSH; the installation sets the available NPSH.

sections.heading: Dimensional analysis
sections.text: Similarity needs geometric, kinematic and dynamic similarity. Key groups are Reynolds number Re = ρVD/μ and relative roughness ε/D for pipes, and specific speed N_s = N√Q ÷ H^(3/4) for rotodynamic pumps, though definitions vary. For the same pump at different speeds, the affinity laws give Q ∝ N, H ∝ N² and power P ∝ N³. Codes and acceptance tests differ by country; check the current local standard.

keyPoints: Darcy-Weisbach friction loss is h_f = f (L/D)(V²/2g); minor losses are h_m = K V²/2g.
Pipes in series add losses at the same flow; pipes in parallel share the same loss and add flows.
The operating point is where the pump curve meets the system curve h_sys = h_static + R Q²; select near best efficiency.
Cavitation happens when local pressure drops below vapour pressure; NPSH_A must exceed NPSH required.
Affinity laws for a pump at different speeds: Q ∝ N, H ∝ N², P ∝ N³.
Similarity uses Re = ρVD/μ, ε/D and specific speed; definitions and codes vary by country, so check local standards.

en.title: Control systems
en.short: Modelling mechanical systems, Laplace transforms, transfer functions, stability, root locus and PID tuning.

sections.heading: Modelling and Laplace
sections.text:
Start with a mass m on a spring of stiffness k and a damper of coefficient c. Newton’s second law gives m ẍ + c ẋ + k x = F(t), where x is displacement and F the applied force. Each dot is one derivative with respect to time.

The Laplace transform turns this calculus into algebra. With zero initial conditions, ẋ becomes sX(s) and ẍ becomes s²X(s). The transfer function is output over input: G(s) = X(s)/F(s) = 1/(ms² + cs + k). The roots of its denominator are the poles.

sections.heading: Blocks and feedback
sections.text:
Blocks in series multiply. A forward path G with feedback H gives G/(1 + GH). Setting 1 + G(s)H(s) = 0 gives the characteristic equation; its roots are the closed-loop poles.

Example: m = 2 kg, c = 4 N·s/m, k = 10 N/m, so G = 1/(2s² + 4s + 10). The poles solve s² + 2s + 5 = 0, giving s = −1 ± 2j. Natural frequency ωn = √(k/m) = 2.24 rad/s. Damping ratio ζ = c ÷ (2√(km)) = 4 ÷ 8.94 = 0.45, so the response oscillates and settles slowly.

sections.heading: Stability and PID
sections.text:
A linear system is stable if every pole has a negative real part, that is, lies left of the imaginary axis. The Routh-Hurwitz test checks this from the coefficients without solving for the roots.

PID control acts on the error e = setpoint − measured value: u = Kp e + Ki ∫e dt + Kd de/dt. Kp speeds the response but leaves a steady offset. Ki removes that offset but adds overshoot and can destabilise. Kd damps the response but amplifies sensor noise. Tune on the real plant, not only on the model.

sections.heading: Root locus and frequency
sections.text:
The root locus plots the closed-loop poles as one gain varies. The branches start at the open-loop poles and end at the open-loop zeros or at infinity.

Frequency response plots gain and phase against frequency, usually as a Bode plot. Gain margin and phase margin show how much extra gain or lag the loop can take before it becomes unstable. Ziegler-Nichols rules give starting PID values from a step test or from the ultimate gain; treat them as a starting point, then refine.

keyPoints: A mass-spring-damper gives G(s) = 1/(ms² + cs + k).
Closed-loop transfer function is G/(1 + GH); stability needs all poles left of the imaginary axis.
ωn = √(k/m) and ζ = c ÷ (2√(km)).
PID: u = Kp e + Ki ∫e dt + Kd de/dt.
Root locus traces closed-loop poles as gain changes; Bode plots give gain and phase margins.
Code requirements and professional registration differ by country, so check the current national source.

en.title: Machine design and CAD
en.short: Design process, loads, safety factors, failure theories, fatigue and CAD for manufacture.

sections.heading: Design process and loads
sections.text: Machine design starts with function, constraints and load cases. Loads may be static, repeated, impact or thermal. A load factor increases an uncertain load; a safety factor n is strength ÷ working stress. It covers uncertainty in loads, material and analysis; its value comes from the relevant standard. Codes and standards differ by country and application. For example, pressure vessel rules in the United States (ASME) and Europe (EN) are not the same. Check the current edition and local regulation. Registration also differs; for example, COREN registers engineers in Nigeria.

sections.heading: Failure theories
sections.text: Failure theories compare a multiaxial stress state with strength from a simple test. For ductile metals, the von Mises (distortion energy) criterion is common; Tresca (maximum shear stress) is more conservative. For brittle materials, maximum principal stress or Mohr theory may be used. Principal stresses are the normal stresses on planes with zero shear. Example: a 40 mm solid shaft carries bending moment M = 600 N·m and torque T = 400 N·m. At the surface, σ = 32M ÷ (πd³) = 95.5 N/mm² and τ = 16T ÷ (πd³) = 31.8 N/mm². Then σ_vm = √(σ² + 3τ²) = √(95.5² + 3 × 31.8²) = 110 N/mm². With yield strength 350 N/mm², n = 350 ÷ 110 = 3.2.

sections.heading: Fatigue and manufacture
sections.text: Fatigue is failure under repeated or fluctuating stress, often below yield. An S-N curve plots stress amplitude against cycles to failure. The endurance limit is the stress below which steel appears to survive indefinitely. Stress concentrations (local stress rises at changes of shape), surface finish and mean stress reduce life. The Goodman relation combines alternating stress σa and mean stress σm: σa ÷ Se + σm ÷ Sut = 1 ÷ n, where Se is the endurance limit and Sut is the ultimate tensile strength. Design for manufacture considers tolerances, surface finish, standard sizes, assembly and cost. CAD (computer-aided design) supports this with 3D models, assemblies, drawings and finite element analysis, but the engineer still checks the design against the current standard.

keyPoints: Safety factor n = strength ÷ working stress; its required value comes from the relevant standard, not a universal number.
For ductile metals, von Mises and Tresca are common yield criteria; Tresca is more conservative.
For plane stress, von Mises stress is σ_vm = √(σx² − σxσy + σy² + 3τxy²).
Fatigue can cause failure below yield; the Goodman relation is σa ÷ Se + σm ÷ Sut = 1 ÷ n.
Design for manufacture considers tolerances, surface finish, standard sizes and assembly; CAD supports modelling and analysis.
Design codes and standards differ by country and application; check the current edition and local regulation.

en.title: Tribology: friction, lubrication and wear
en.short: Friction, wear mechanisms, lubrication regimes, viscosity and choosing lubricants for bearings.

sections.heading: Friction
sections.text: Friction is the resistance to relative motion between surfaces in contact. Amontons’ laws state that friction force is proportional to normal load and independent of apparent contact area: F = μN, where μ is the coefficient of friction. Real surfaces touch only at asperities (tiny bumps on the surface), so the true contact area is small and grows with load. Static friction is usually higher than kinetic friction. Friction wastes energy as heat, but brakes, clutches and belts depend on it.

sections.heading: Wear mechanisms
sections.text: Wear is loss of material from surfaces. The main mechanisms are adhesive wear, where asperities weld and tear away; abrasive wear, from hard particles cutting the surface, often modelled by Archard’s equation V = kWL ÷ H, where V is worn volume, W load, L sliding distance, H hardness and k a wear coefficient; fatigue wear, from repeated rolling loads causing pitting; and corrosive or erosive wear. Harder surfaces and clean lubricant reduce wear.

sections.heading: Regimes and viscosity
sections.text:
Viscosity is a fluid’s resistance to shear. Dynamic viscosity μ (Pa·s) links shear stress to shear rate: τ = μ du/dy. Kinematic viscosity ν = μ ÷ ρ is in m²/s, often mm²/s (cSt). Viscosity falls as temperature rises, so oils are sold in viscosity classes; check supplier data at the working temperature.

The regimes are boundary (surfaces touch, additives do the work), mixed (part contact, part film), hydrodynamic (a full film separates the surfaces) and elastohydrodynamic (thin film with elastic flattening, as in rolling bearings). The Stribeck curve plots friction against a lubrication parameter and shows these regimes.

sections.heading: Bearing lubrication and selection
sections.text:
In a plain journal bearing the shaft sits slightly off-centre; oil dragged into the converging gap builds pressure that carries the load. Friction rises with viscosity and speed and falls with clearance, but too much clearance loses the film.

Example: μ = 0.05 Pa·s, U = 3 m/s, h = 50 μm, A = 0.02 m².
τ = μU ÷ h = 0.05 × 3 ÷ 0.00005 = 3000 Pa
F = τA = 3000 × 0.02 = 60 N

Match viscosity to speed and load; use extreme-pressure additives for boundary contact and grease where sealing is hard. Standards vary by country and manufacturer.

keyPoints: Friction force is F = μN; it depends on load and the surface pair, not apparent area.
Archard’s equation V = kWL ÷ H estimates abrasive wear volume.
Dynamic viscosity is defined by τ = μ du/dy; kinematic viscosity ν = μ ÷ ρ.
The four regimes are boundary, mixed, hydrodynamic and elastohydrodynamic.
Viscosity falls as temperature rises, so choose a grade at the working temperature.
Film shear stress is τ = μU ÷ h, and friction force is τA.

en.title: Refrigeration and air conditioning
en.short: Vapour compression and absorption cycles, heat pumps, refrigerants, psychrometrics and cooling load.

sections.heading: Vapour compression
sections.text:
A vapour compression refrigerator circulates a refrigerant through compressor, condenser, expansion valve and evaporator. The compressor raises pressure and temperature; the condenser rejects heat; the expansion valve drops pressure; the evaporator absorbs heat from the cooled space. Coefficient of performance COP = useful cooling ÷ compressor work. Using enthalpies h, COP = (h1 − h4) ÷ (h2 − h1), where 1 is evaporator outlet, 2 compressor outlet and 4 expansion valve outlet.

Example: h1 = 250, h2 = 290 and h4 = 80 kJ/kg. COP = (250 − 80) ÷ (290 − 250) = 170 ÷ 40 = 4.25.

sections.heading: Absorption and heat pumps
sections.text: Absorption refrigeration replaces the compressor with a pump and heat input. A pair such as ammonia-water or lithium bromide-water is used. It is driven by heat, so it suits waste heat or solar heat. A heat pump uses the same vapour compression cycle but delivers condenser heat. Its COP is heating delivered ÷ compressor work, often above 1 because it moves heat rather than creating it.

sections.heading: Refrigerants
sections.text: Refrigerants are chosen for pressure, latent heat, safety, toxicity, flammability and environmental effect. Older CFCs damaged the ozone layer; HFCs are ozone-safe but are greenhouse gases. Rules differ by country and change, so check current national regulations.

sections.heading: Psychrometrics and cooling load
sections.text: Psychrometrics deals with moist air. Dry-bulb temperature is ordinary temperature; wet-bulb is reached by evaporative cooling; relative humidity is vapour pressure ÷ saturation vapour pressure at the same temperature. Specific humidity is mass of water vapour per mass of dry air. On a psychrometric chart, sensible cooling moves left at constant humidity ratio; dehumidification lowers humidity ratio. Cooling load is heat that must be removed. Sensible heat Q = m cp ΔT. Example: 1 kg/s air cooled from 30 to 20 °C with cp = 1.005 kJ/kgK gives Q = 1 × 1.005 × 10 = 10.05 kW. Air conditioning processes include heating, cooling, humidifying, dehumidifying and filtration.

keyPoints: COP of a vapour compression cycle is (h1 − h4) ÷ (h2 − h1).
Absorption refrigeration is driven by heat, not a compressor.
Heat pump COP is heating delivered ÷ compressor work.
Refrigerant choice depends on safety and environmental rules, which vary by country.
Relative humidity is vapour pressure ÷ saturation vapour pressure at the same temperature.
Sensible cooling load is Q = m cp ΔT; add latent heat for moisture removal.

en.title: Industrial engineering and maintenance
en.short: Production planning, work study, quality, reliability, maintenance, lean and plant safety.

sections.heading: Planning and work study
sections.text: Production planning decides what to make, how much and when. It links demand forecasting, aggregate planning, the master production schedule and material requirements planning (MRP), then checks capacity. Work study has method study, which improves how work is done, and work measurement, which sets standard time: normal time = observed time × rating factor; standard time = normal time × (1 + allowance). Example: observed 8.0 min, rating 110%, allowance 15%. Normal time = 8.0 × 1.10 = 8.8 min. Standard time = 8.8 × 1.15 = 10.12 min. Allowances cover rest, personal needs and delays.

sections.heading: Quality and reliability
sections.text: Quality control checks that products meet requirements. Statistical process control plots measurements on control charts; points outside control limits or non-random patterns signal special causes. Acceptance sampling decides whether to accept a lot from a sample, with sampling risks. Reliability is the probability that an item performs its function for a stated time under stated conditions. For constant failure rate λ, reliability R = e^(−λt) and mean time between failures MTBF = 1 ÷ λ. Example: λ = 0.0002 per hour, t = 1000 h, R = e^(−0.2) = 0.819.

sections.heading: Maintenance strategies
sections.text: Reactive maintenance repairs after failure. Preventive maintenance services at fixed intervals. Predictive or condition-based maintenance acts on measured condition, such as vibration, oil analysis or temperature. Corrective maintenance restores a failed item. Reliability-centred maintenance chooses tasks by failure consequence, and total productive maintenance involves operators in basic care. Maintenance planning needs spares, schedules and records. The best mix depends on failure mode, downtime cost and safety risk.

sections.heading: Lean and safety
sections.text: Lean seeks value and removes waste: waiting, inventory, overproduction, defects, motion, transport and overprocessing. Just-in-time and kanban pull material when needed, but need dependable suppliers and processes. Safety starts with hazard identification and risk assessment: likelihood and severity. Controls follow a hierarchy: remove the hazard, guard or isolate it, then procedures and training, with protective equipment last. Legal duties differ by country, so check national law and site rules.

keyPoints: Production planning links demand forecasting, master scheduling, MRP and capacity checks.
Normal time = observed time × rating factor; standard time = normal time × (1 + allowance).
Control charts separate common and special cause variation, while acceptance sampling uses sampling risks.
For constant failure rate, R = e^(−λt) and MTBF = 1 ÷ λ.
Preventive maintenance is time-based; predictive maintenance is condition-based.
Lean removes waste, and safety controls hazards by hierarchy, with legal duties varying by country.

en.title: Professional practice, ethics and registration
en.short: Ethics, contracts, liability, codes and standards, and engineering registration.

sections.heading: Ethics and conduct
sections.text:
Engineering ethics is the set of principles that guides decisions when safety, honesty and public welfare compete with cost or loyalty. Professional bodies publish codes of ethics. Common duties are to work within competence, be honest, protect health and safety, keep confidentiality, declare conflicts of interest and refuse bribery. A code is not a law, but breach can lead to discipline and loss of registration.

Case: Ngozi, a mechanical engineer in Lagos, is asked by her manager Musa to approve a pressure vessel without test records. She should refuse and report the gap, not sign.

sections.heading: Contracts and liability
sections.text:
In common-law systems, a contract usually needs offer, acceptance, consideration (something of value exchanged) and intention to be legally bound. Engineering contracts set scope, price, time, variations, payment and dispute resolution. Standard forms such as FIDIC (used worldwide), NEC and JCT (both from the UK) are common but differ.

Liability may arise in contract or in tort (a civil wrong), especially negligence: a duty of care, breach, causation and loss. Professionals manage risk with clear records, limitation clauses and professional indemnity insurance (cover for claims). Insurance does not replace competent work.

sections.heading: Codes and standards
sections.text:
Technical codes and standards are agreed rules for design, materials, testing and safety. ISO is international; ASME is from the United States; BS and EN are British and European; NIS (Nigerian Industrial Standards) is Nigerian. They differ in assumptions, units and scope, and editions change.

A design that satisfies one country’s regulator may not satisfy another. Use the edition named in the contract and check the current official source.

sections.heading: Registration
sections.text:
Registration or licensure is legal permission to practise as an engineer. In Nigeria, COREN (Council for the Regulation of Engineering in Nigeria) regulates engineering and registers engineers. Other examples are the Engineering Council in the United Kingdom, ECSA (Engineering Council of South Africa), Engineers Canada with provincial regulators, and state licensing boards in the United States.

Requirements and titles differ by country. Check the current regulator for fees, examinations and continuing professional development.

keyPoints: Engineering ethics puts public safety, honesty and competence before cost or loyalty.
In common-law systems, a contract usually needs offer, acceptance, consideration and intention to be legally bound.
Professional liability can arise from breach of contract or negligence, so keep records and carry suitable insurance.
ISO, ASME, BS/EN and NIS standards differ; use the edition required by the contract and check the current official source.
In Nigeria, COREN regulates engineering registration; equivalent bodies exist in other countries.
Registration requirements, titles and codes vary by country and year, so confirm them with the current regulator.

en.title: Engineering project planning and technical communication
en.short: Planning a final-year project, searching literature, handling data, writing reports and presenting.

sections.heading: Planning the project
sections.text: A project plan states the aim, scope, deliverables, milestones and risks. The aim is the question the work answers. Scope lists what is included and excluded. Deliverables are what you hand in, such as a rig, data and report. Milestones are decision dates. A Gantt chart shows tasks against time; a risk register lists what may go wrong and your response. In a team, agree roles, keep meeting notes and use one shared file store. Example: Ada and Musa plan a solar dryer test, fix variables, book the balance and set a draft-report date.

sections.heading: Literature and methods
sections.text: Search with keywords, then follow citations from good papers. Use primary sources such as journal papers and standards, and secondary sources such as textbooks. Record each source as you read. For an experiment, define variables, controls, calibration and repeats. For a design, state requirements and constraints, compare concepts, then verify the chosen design. In Nigeria, COREN regulates engineering practice; other countries have their own bodies. Cite the code edition and country, and do not quote clause numbers unless checked.

sections.heading: Data and reports
sections.text: Keep raw data in a log with date, units, instrument and observer. Check outliers, but never delete a reading without a reason. Use tables and graphs with units and captions. A technical report usually has an abstract, introduction, method, results, discussion, conclusion and references. The discussion explains what results mean and their uncertainty. Referencing follows your department’s style, such as Harvard or IEEE, and every borrowed idea needs a citation. Plagiarism includes copying text, figures or data without credit.

sections.heading: Presenting and teamwork
sections.text: An oral presentation has a short opening, a clear question, the method, key results and a conclusion. Put few words on each slide and practise to time. Expect questions and answer briefly. In teams, keep a decision log and a shared folder with version names. Review each other’s work before submission. A check: could a reader who was not in the laboratory repeat the work from your report?

keyPoints: Define aim, scope, deliverables, milestones and risks before starting.
Use primary sources and record every reference as you read it.
State variables, controls, calibration and repeats for experiments; requirements and verification for designs.
Keep raw data with units and never delete readings without a reason.
Follow the required referencing style and cite every borrowed idea.
Rehearse the talk to time and keep team decisions in a shared log.

en.title: Advanced solid mechanics and the finite element method
en.short: Continuum stress and strain, yield and plasticity, and the finite element method for solids.

sections.heading: Stress and strain
sections.text: Stress at a point is a tensor with three normal and three shear components, σij. Strain εij measures deformation and, for small strains, is linear in the displacement gradients. For an isotropic material Hooke’s law needs only Young’s modulus E and Poisson’s ratio ν. Principal stresses are the eigenvalues of the stress tensor and act on planes carrying no shear.

sections.heading: Yield and plasticity
sections.text:
A yield criterion marks the end of elastic behaviour. Metals commonly follow von Mises, where yielding begins when the second deviatoric invariant J2 reaches a critical value; Tresca instead uses maximum shear stress. In uniaxial tension both reduce to σ = σY, the yield strength.

Past yield, an elastic-perfectly plastic model holds stress constant as strain grows, while hardening models expand the yield surface. Plastic strain is irreversible, so results depend on the loading path.

sections.heading: Finite element method
sections.text:
The domain is divided into elements joined at nodes. Shape functions interpolate displacement from nodal values, giving the element stiffness Ke = ∫ Bᵀ D B dV, where B relates strain to nodal displacement and D is the elasticity matrix. Assembly gives Ku = F, solved for displacements, then strains and stresses.

Example: a bar element with E = 200,000 N/mm², A = 100 mm², L = 500 mm.
k = EA ÷ L = 200,000 × 100 ÷ 500 = 40,000 N/mm
With F = 8,000 N: u = 8,000 ÷ 40,000 = 0.2 mm
Check: σ = F ÷ A = 80 N/mm², ε = 80 ÷ 200,000 = 4 × 10⁻⁴, u = εL = 0.2 mm.

sections.heading: Meshing and validation
sections.text: Choose elements to suit the physics: solid elements for thick three-dimensional parts, shell and beam elements for thin or slender ones, with order and integration matched to the strain gradients. Refine the mesh until results change little; that is convergence. Boundary conditions must remove rigid body motion without over-constraining the model. Validate against a closed-form solution, a hand calculation or measured data, and report the comparison.

keyPoints: Stress and strain are tensors; for an isotropic material Hooke’s law needs only E and ν.
Von Mises yielding depends on the second deviatoric invariant J2 and gives σ = σY in uniaxial tension.
Element stiffness is Ke = ∫ Bᵀ D B dV, and assembly gives Ku = F.
For a bar element k = EA ÷ L; with E = 200,000 N/mm², A = 100 mm² and L = 500 mm, k = 40,000 N/mm.
Refine the mesh until results converge, then validate against analytical or experimental results.
Design codes and registration differ by country (for example COREN in Nigeria); check the current official source.

en.title: Computational fluid dynamics
en.short: Governing equations, discretisation, boundary conditions, turbulence, stability, and verification of CFD results.

sections.heading: Governing equations
sections.text: CFD solves the conservation laws for mass, momentum and energy on a mesh. For incompressible flow, mass conservation is ∇·u = 0. Momentum conservation is ρ(∂u/∂t + u·∇u) = −∇p + μ∇²u + f, the Navier-Stokes equation. Energy adds temperature and heat transfer. The Reynolds number Re = ρUL/μ compares inertia with viscosity; high Re makes turbulence important. These equations rarely have analytic solutions for practical geometry, so they are approximated numerically.

sections.heading: Discretisation and stability
sections.text: Discretisation replaces derivatives by algebraic relations on cells or nodes. The finite volume method integrates over each cell and is common in engineering CFD because it conserves mass and momentum. A first-order upwind scheme is stable but diffusive; higher-order schemes are more accurate but can oscillate. Time stepping must satisfy stability limits. For explicit advection, the Courant number C = uΔt/Δx should generally be at most about 1; exact limits depend on the scheme. Too large a time step causes unbounded growth, not a better answer.

sections.heading: Boundary conditions and turbulence
sections.text: Boundary conditions define the problem: inlet velocity, outlet pressure, walls with no slip, and symmetry. Wrong or poorly placed boundaries change the whole solution. Turbulence modelling is needed because resolving every eddy is too costly. Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) models, such as k-ε, solve averaged equations with a turbulence model; large eddy simulation (LES) resolves large eddies and models small ones. Each model has limits.

sections.heading: Verification and validation
sections.text: Verification checks that equations are solved correctly, for example by mesh refinement and comparison with exact solutions. Validation checks the model against experiments. A mesh independence study shows that further refinement changes results little.
